title: Causal Mask in a Transformer Decoder
body:
A transformer decoder processes a sentence token by token. Each token forms a query that compares to all keys produced from earlier tokens.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Causal mask on decoder scores","caption":"The mask hides later keys so each position only attends to itself and earlier positions.","kind":"heatmap","rowLabel":"Query position","columnLabel":"Key position","columns":["the 1","cat 2","sat 3","on 4","the 5","mat 6"],"rows":[{"label":"the 1","cells":[1.209,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"cat 2","cells":[0.496,3.33,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"sat 3","cells":[-0.381,2.145,0.923,null,null,null]},{"label":"on 4","cells":[-0.685,-0.528,-0.706,-0.588,null,null]},{"label":"the 5","cells":[-0.479,-0.893,-0.776,-0.427,-0.255,null]},{"label":"mat 6","cells":[0.387,0.396,0.452,0.335,0.338,0.208]}],"range":{"min":-4,"max":4}}}
```

The heatmap shows raw attention scores before masking. Blank cells (null) are where later keys are hidden. After applying the causal mask, only the upper‑left triangle remains.

The mask sets those later‑key scores to $-\,\infty$, so the softmax turns them into zero weight. Consequently, the decoder can only attend to itself and previous tokens, never to future words.

This mechanism enforces the autoregressive property needed for language generation, ensuring predictions depend solely on already generated output.

title: Causal Masking in Transformer Decoder
body:
The decoder computes attention scores for each query token against all key tokens. To prevent using future information, a causal mask adds $-\,\infty$ to any score where the key index $j$ exceeds the query index $i$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"heatmap","title":"Causal mask before softmax","caption":"Gray cells are blocked (‑∞) so later keys get zero weight.","rowLabel":"Query position","columnLabel":"Key position","columns":["1","2","3","4","5","6"],"rows":[{"label":"1","cells":[null,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"2","cells":[0,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"3","cells":[0,0,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"4","cells":[0,0,0,null,null,null]},{"label":"5","cells":[0,0,0,0,null,null]},{"label":"6","cells":[0,0,0,0,0,null]}],"range":{"min":0,"max":1}}}
```

After adding the mask, the softmax normalises only the allowed scores, yielding a probability distribution that sums to 1 for each row. Consequently, each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens.

The mask is a binary matrix: entry $(i,j)$ is 0 (allowed) when $j\le i$ and $-\infty$ (blocked) otherwise. This simple rule enforces the autoregressive property required for language generation.

title: Forward Diffusion with Known Noise
body:
Consider a 2×2 latent grid at a diffusion step. The clean values (first column) are mixed with a known noise pattern (second column) using the diffusion coefficients for that step.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"heatmap","title":"Forward diffusion with known noise (illustrative)","caption":"Each cell shows the contribution of clean latent and known noise to the noisy result.","rowLabel":"Cell","columnLabel":"Component","columns":["Clean latent","Known noise","Noisy result"],"rows":[{"label":"Top‑left","cells":[0.8,-0.5,0.34]},{"label":"Top‑right","cells":[0.2,0.5,0.46]},{"label":"Bottom‑left","cells":[0.2,-0.25,0.01]},{"label":"Bottom‑right","cells":[0.8,0.25,0.79]}],"range":{"min":-1,"max":1}}}
```

The noisy result (third column) is computed as \(x_{t}=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\). Here \(\sqrt{\alpha_t}=0.8\) and \(\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}=0.5\) for illustration, giving the numbers shown.

The heatmap makes it easy to see how each cell’s clean part and noise part combine to the final noisy value.

title: Gini Impurity and Information Gain
body:
We compute Gini impurity to measure how often a randomly chosen element would be incorrectly labeled. For a node with proportions $p_i$, the impurity is $1 - \sum p_i^2$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

Notice how the left child is pure with a Gini of $0$, while the right child has mixed classes with a Gini of $0.375$. We weigh these child impurities by their fraction of samples to find the total split impurity.

Information gain is then the parent's impurity minus this weighted average child impurity. Maximizing this gain is how decision trees decide where to split data.

prompt: how do I compute the Gini impurity on both sides of a split and the information gain?
title: Gini Impurity and Information Gain
body:
To find how well a split separates data, we measure Gini impurity, which is $1 - \sum p_i^2$ for each node.

Suppose a root node splits into two equal groups where the left has four items of class zero and the right has one item of class zero and three of class one.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine the child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

For the left child, the Gini is $1 - (1)^2 - 0 = 0$. For the right child, the Gini is $1 - (1/4)^2 - (3/4)^2 = 0.375$. We combine these using their weights to get the weighted impurity of $0.1875$.

Information gain is the parent impurity minus this weighted child impurity. It tells us how much certainty the split adds to our classification tree.

prompt: how do I compute the Gini impurity on both sides of a split and the information gain?
title: Computing Gini impurity and information gain
body:
Consider splitting eight data points into two equally sized children. To measure class mix, we compute the Gini impurity $1 - \sum p_i^2$ for each side.

Look for the child metrics in the split table above to trace each calculation. The left child holds four points of class zero, giving a Gini of zero.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine the child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

The right child holds one point of class zero and three of class one, giving $1 - (1/4)^2 - (3/4)^2 = 0.375$.

We combine them via weighted average to get the split impurity: $0.5(0) + 0.5(0.375) = 0.1875$. Information gain is the parent impurity minus this weighted child impurity.
